disposition: CONFIRMED -- as filed, and the cost is larger than the ticket states
the_ticket_claimed: a transient filesystem error during a protocol write is escalated to a blocking content conflict, contradicting the contract and doing so silently

what_is_measured.how_the_transient_error_is_forced: .saipen/STATE.md is opened with open(path,'r+b') and held for the duration of one CLI subprocess call, then closed. Win32 opens without FILE_SHARE_DELETE by default, so os.replace on that target fails with WinError 5 -- the same failure an antivirus scanner, a search indexer or a second writer produces. No timing race is involved and the lock is provably gone before the next step.
what_is_measured.control: the same transition with no lock returns TRANSITIONED, so the path and the harness are sound

the_full_session.step: transition VERIFY with the lock held
the_full_session.detail: target .saipen/STATE.md action failed: [WinError 5] Access is denied

the_full_session.step: lock released; the IDENTICAL command retried, same bytes, nothing else changed
the route the engine itself named: accept_live
the_full_session.detail: resolving to current live leaves an invalid repository: STATE proposed last_event 3 != LOG tail 4

the_full_session.step: the route the engine does NOT name: bare saipen recover

what_is_measured.operator_session_shape: 4 commands where 1 was intended; 2 of the 4 are spent on the branch the engine itself named

the_two_branches_are_the_same_answer.reading: ten lines apart in journal.py, byte-identical in every field a caller can branch on. The only textual difference is the detail string: 'action failed: <OSError>' versus 'action left <hash>, expected <hash>'.

what_the_ticket_missed.the_real_cost_is_not_the_label: calling an I/O failure a content conflict costs three extra commands for a condition that was over before the retry. That is real but survivable.
what_the_ticket_missed.the_unrecoverable_cost_is_the_routing: the RECOVERY_CONFLICT refusal carries canonical_next_command naming `recover resolve --resolution <accept_live|replan>`. Measured in this very state, BOTH of those routes answer NEEDS_REPAIR. The bare `saipen recover` -- the one route that settles it -- is named nowhere in any answer. So the engine routes the operator, by its own canonical command, into the dead-end branch and away from the working one.
what_the_ticket_missed.and_that_is_T_1398: T-1398 measured the same dead-end in the same shape and found it is total when a third party has also written an applied target. T-1394 is therefore not merely cosmetic: it is the most likely way a normal Windows session walks into T-1398's deadlock, and it hands the operator a map to the one route that cannot get them out.

recurrence: any Windows process holding a short lock on a protocol target -- an antivirus scanner, a search indexer, an editor with the file open, or a second session on the same tree. These are routine, not adversarial, and none of them indicates contention over content.

the_minimum_fix.preferred: one line at journal.py:3055 -- mark the journal CONFLICT as today (the op IS half-applied, so refusing to proceed is correct) but give the refusal a canonical_next_command that names the bare `saipen recover`, which re-derives each target from live bytes and settles the clean case without a human. This changes no safety property: it only stops the engine from recommending a branch measured not to work.
the_minimum_fix.the_larger_alternative: return a distinct code from the OSError branch (for example IO_BLOCKED with recovery_required false) so that a plain retry works, because the bytes may be perfectly fine. This is better UX but it changes admission semantics, and a genuinely half-applied op must not admit a new mutation -- so it needs its own design, not a one-liner.
the_minimum_fix.which_to_choose: the preferred fix. The engine's refusal is right; only its advice is wrong.

measured: the OSError branch returns code CONFLICT and recovery_required true, identical literals to the content-mismatch branch ten lines below
the lock is released before the retry, and the identical command is still refused with RECOVERY_CONFLICT
canonical_next_command on that refusal names recover resolve --resolution accept_live|replan
both named routes answer NEEDS_REPAIR in this state
the bare saipen recover answers RECOVERED and the retry then succeeds
inferred: that an antivirus scanner or indexer produces the same WinError 5 -- standard Win32 behaviour for a handle without FILE_SHARE_DELETE, and the reason T-1398's harness uses it, but not observed from an actual scanner in this run
not_established: how often this fires in a real project; no incident log in this repository counts it
whether the engine would eventually self-heal if the operator simply kept retrying; the retry is refused outright, so nothing was observed

why_not_fixed_here: the change is in the SAIPEN engine repo (journal.py:3054 and the refusal's canonical_next_command in saipen.py). That repo has 1750 dirty tracked files and another live session's uncommitted work; editing it would sweep that work into a commit. Measured and filed; the patch is not applied blind.
engine_is_untouched: every step is the public CLI in a subprocess with --project-root pointed at build/t1394/scratch. journal.py was read, never written.
